title: The future
intro: This unit adds the future tense `-(y)AcAk`: *Yarın ne yapacaksın?* (What will you do tomorrow?) *Annemi arayacağım* (I'll call my mother). It covers the forms, the negative and the question, the four verbs whose stems change, and how the future shares the work of talking about plans with the present continuous.

blocks.text: The future tense (*gelecek zaman*) is built like the present continuous: the stem, the tense suffix `-(y)AcAk`, and the type I endings you know from **to be** (see [the two sets](gp-person-endings-types)): *gel-* + *-ecek* + *-im* → *geleceğim* (I will come).

blocks.label: Future
lines: k → ğ  before a vowel     geleceğim, yapacağız

blocks.text: **Harmony.** Both vowels of `-AcAk` follow two-way harmony: *-ecek* after e, i, ö, ü; *-acak* after a, ı, o, u: *gelecek*, *görecek*, *yapacak*, *okuyacak*.
**Buffer y.** After a stem ending in a vowel, a y comes in: *oku-* → *okuyacak*, *bekle-* → *bekleyecek*, *anla-* → *anlayacak*. The stem's own vowel stays in writing: *bekleyecek*, *anlayacak*.

**k → ğ.** The final k softens to ğ before a vowel, so before the endings for **I** and **we**: *geleceğim*, *geleceğiz*. Before an ending that starts with a consonant it stays: *geleceksin*, *gelecekler*. It is the same softening you know from *kitap* → *kitabı* ([A1 unit 8](gp-consonant-softening)).

blocks.text: **To be in the future.** `-(y)AcAk` goes on verbs only, so **will be** uses *olmak*: *Yarın evde olacağım* (I'll be at home tomorrow), *Hava güzel olacak* (The weather will be nice).

items.en: What will you do tomorrow?
I'll call my mother.
We're going to watch a film this evening.
The bus will leave in five minutes.
I think it's going to rain.
I'll be at home tomorrow.

blocks.text: Write the stem's vowel before the y as it is: *bekleyecek*, *anlayacak*, *söyleyecek*. In speech they often sound like *bekliyecek*, but in writing only *de-* and *ye-* change (see the third section).
In casual speech the future is shortened: *yapacağım* sounds like *yapıcam*, *geleceğim* like *gelicem*, *ne yapacaksın?* like *napıcan?* You'll hear it all the time; write the full forms.

sections.title: Gelmeyeceğim, gelecek misin? Negative and questions

blocks.text: **Negative.** Put `-mA` after the stem, then a buffer y, then `-AcAk`: *gel-* + *-me-* + *-y-* + *-eceğ-* + *-im* → *gelmeyeceğim* (I won't come). The e or a of `-mA` follows two-way harmony and stays in writing: *gelmeyecek*, *yapmayacak*.

**Questions.** The future works like `-(I)yor`, not like `-DI`: the personal ending moves onto `mI`, which follows the vowel of `-AcAk`: *Gelecek misin?* (Will you come?), *Yapacak mısınız?* Before the particle the k stays k. For **they**, *-lAr* stays on the verb: *Gelecekler mi?*

items.en: Will you come tomorrow?
Don't worry, I won't forget.
Is it going to rain tomorrow?
Will you be at home this evening?
Aren't you going to have a coffee?
The children won't go to school this week.

blocks.text: The ending goes on the particle: *gelecek misin?*, not *geleceksin mi?* And in writing the negative keeps its e or a: *gelmeyecek*, *yapmayacak*, never *gelmiyecek*, even though that is how it often sounds.
Three tenses, two patterns for questions. Type I tenses move the ending onto `mI`: *geliyor musun?*, *gelecek misin?* The type II past keeps it on the verb: *geldin mi?*
Four verbs change their stem before `-(y)AcAk`, the same four that change before `-(I)yor` ([A1 unit 6](gp-present-continuous)):

items: *de-* (say) and *ye-* (eat) turn their e into i before the buffer y: *diyecek*, *yiyecek*.
*git-* (go) and *et-* (do) turn their t into d before the vowel: *gidecek*, *edecek*. Every phrase with *etmek* does the same: *yardım edecek*, *dans edecek*, *teşekkür edeceğim*.

blocks.text: The negative keeps the stem as it is, because `-mA` starts with a consonant: *demeyecek*, *yemeyecek*, *gitmeyecek*, *etmeyecek*.

items.en: What will you say?
What are we going to eat this evening?
I'm going to Izmir tomorrow.
I'll help you.
Aren't you going to eat?

blocks.text: Only *de-* and *ye-* change their vowel: *bekleyecek*, *söyleyecek*, *dinleyecek* keep theirs. And most other verbs in t keep the t: *bitecek* (it will end), *yatacak* (will lie down).
*Yiyecek* is also a noun, **food**, and *gelecek* a noun, **the future**: *Gelecekte ne olacak?* (What will happen in the future?)
Turkish has two ways to talk about plans, much as English has **I'll go**, **I'm going to go** and **I'm going**.

items: **An arrangement already made**, usually with a time word: `-(I)yor`. *Yarın İzmir'e gidiyorum* (I'm going to Izmir tomorrow: the ticket is booked).
**An intention or decision**: `-(y)AcAk`. *Bu yaz Türkçe öğreneceğim* (This summer I'm going to learn Turkish).
**A prediction**: `-(y)AcAk`. *Galiba yağmur yağacak* (I think it's going to rain), *Geç kalacağız* (We'll be late).
**A timetable or announcement**: either. *Tren dokuzda kalkacak* or *kalkıyor* (The train leaves at nine).

blocks.text: Often both are possible and the difference is small: *Haftaya Ankara'ya gidiyoruz* sounds settled, *Haftaya Ankara'ya gideceğiz* states the plan. A quick promise or offer made on the spot (**I'll call you**) takes a third tense, the aorist of [unit 4](gp-aorist-uses): *Seni ararım*.

**… sonra, in.** After a number and a time word, *sonra* means **in** (from now): *iki gün sonra*, *beş dakika sonra*. It mirrors *önce*, **ago**, from [unit 1](gp-time-past). (*Sonra* after the ablative, *yemekten sonra*, means **after**: [unit 9](gp-postp-ablative).)

*Haftaya* (next week) and *seneye* (next year) are a week and a year with the dative: literally **to the week**. *Sene* is another word for *yıl*, year. Both can be followed by a day: *haftaya salı* (Tuesday next week).

items.en: We're going to Ankara next week.
I'm going to finish university next year.
What are you going to do next week?
What are you doing this evening?
The train will leave in half an hour.
Maybe it will snow tomorrow.

blocks.text: English **will** and **going to** both come out as `-(y)AcAk`, and English **I'm going** for a fixed plan matches `-(I)yor`. French spreads the same ground over its futur (j'irai), futur proche (je vais aller) and present (je pars demain).
*Gelecek* means **next** before a time word (*gelecek hafta*, *gelecek yaz*), and *geçen* means **last**: *geçen hafta*, *gelecek hafta*.

summary: Future: stem + `-(y)AcAk` + type I ending: *geleceğim, geleceksin, gelecek, geleceğiz, geleceksiniz, gelecekler*.
Two-way harmony (*-ecek, -acak*), a buffer y after vowels (*okuyacak*), and k → ğ before a vowel (*yapacağım*).
Negative `-mA` + y: *gelmeyeceğim*. Question: the ending moves onto `mI`: *Gelecek misin?*, but *Gelecekler mi?*
*De-* and *ye-* become *diyecek*, *yiyecek*; *git-* and *et-* become *gidecek*, *edecek*. The negative keeps the stem: *gitmeyecek*.
Fixed arrangements often take `-(I)yor` (*Yarın gidiyorum*); intentions and predictions take `-(y)AcAk` (*Yağmur yağacak*).
Time words: *yarın*, *öbür gün*, *haftaya*, *seneye*, *gelecek hafta*, and *… sonra* for **in**: *iki gün sonra*.
